Jibrin W.lab_name: Diabetes, Endocrinology and Reproductive Biology, School of Medicine, University of Dundee (Dundee, Scotland, United Kingdom)
Jibrin W.role: Researcher at the University of Dundee School of Medicine who led a 2026 cell-culture test of whether rapamycin can shield sperm-precursor cells from the cancer drug cisplatin
Jibrin W.sub: School of Medicine, University of Dundee (at the time of the study, 2026)
story: Cisplatin is a platinum-based chemotherapy drug used against many childhood and adult cancers. It kills dividing cells, and that includes the cells in the testis that will later make sperm, so boys treated for cancer can become infertile as adults. In mouse ovaries, earlier work had suggested that rapamycin, a drug that switches off mTOR (the cell's growth-control kinase), can put egg-cell precursors into a quieter state and protect them from chemotherapy. Wafiya Jibrin was first author of the 2026 Atlas study that asked whether the same trick works for the male side (JIB2026).

The team exposed GC6-spg cells, a mouse cell line that behaves like spermatogonia (the stem-like cells that give rise to sperm), to cisplatin with and without rapamycin. Rapamycin did not reduce the damage. The result is a useful negative one: a protective strategy reported in female fertility models cannot simply be carried over to the testis. It was shown only in a cell line in a dish, not in animals or in patients.

The study came from Federica Lopes's group in the School of Medicine at the University of Dundee, which works on fertility preservation for young cancer patients. PubMed lists no other papers under this name, and no institutional page could be found, so the Dundee affiliation shown is the one on the 2026 paper.

highlights.JIB2026: First author: tested rapamycin as a shield for a mouse spermatogonial cell line exposed to cisplatin and found that it gave no protection.

Jibrin W.note: No web or ORCID record found; only one PubMed paper. Position and career stage (student or staff) unconfirmed.

Lopes F.lab_name: Diabetes, Endocrinology and Reproductive Biology, School of Medicine, University of Dundee (Dundee, Scotland, United Kingdom)
Lopes F.role: Reproductive biologist and Lecturer at the University of Dundee who studies how chemotherapy damages the immature testis and ovary, with the aim of protecting the future fertility of children treated for cancer
Lopes F.sub: Lecturer, Diabetes, Endocrinology and Reproductive Biology, School of Medicine, University of Dundee · earlier research at the University of Edinburgh (Biomedical Sciences and MRC Centre for Reproductive Health, papers 2013–2022)
story: Federica Lopes was senior author of the 2026 Atlas study (JIB2026) that tested whether rapamycin, a drug that switches off mTOR, could protect sperm-precursor cells from cisplatin. In female fertility models, earlier reports had suggested that rapamycin keeps egg-cell precursors in a resting state and so spares them from chemotherapy. In this study, done on a mouse spermatogonial cell line (GC6-spg) in a dish, rapamycin gave no protection. The finding warns against assuming that a fertility-sparing drug which helps the ovary will also help the testis.

The question fits a long line of Lopes's own work. At the University of Edinburgh, working with Norah Spears and Rod Mitchell, Lopes cultured whole prepubertal mouse testes and ovaries and exposed them to cancer drugs at doses seen in patients. These studies showed that the irinotecan metabolite SN38 killed germ cells in the young testis but spared the ovary (2016), that carboplatin is no less damaging to young gonads than the older drug cisplatin (2020), and that a single exposure to cisplatin or doxorubicin harms spermatogonial stem cells and lowers sperm production weeks later (2020). Work on human fetal and prepubertal testis tissue then showed that the supporting Sertoli cells survive platinum drugs, which keeps open the option of restoring fertility by stem-cell transplant (2022).

Lopes is now a Lecturer in Diabetes, Endocrinology and Reproductive Biology at the University of Dundee School of Medicine, where the university lists a PhD project on fertility preservation for boys with cancer. Recent Dundee papers also cover embryo culture conditions in the IVF laboratory (2025) and access to fertility care in low- and middle-income countries (2024).

highlights.JIB2026: Senior author: led the Dundee study showing that rapamycin did not protect a mouse spermatogonial cell line from cisplatin damage.

Lopes F.note: PhD and early training not found on the Dundee page.

Qiu Z.lab_name: School of Pharmacy, Hubei University of Chinese Medicine (Wuhan, Hubei, China)
Qiu Z.role: Pharmacologist and Professor at Hubei University of Chinese Medicine who studies how natural medicines act on liver and kidney disease, including fatty liver disease and drug-induced organ damage
Qiu Z.sub: Professor and doctoral supervisor, School of Pharmacy, Hubei University of Chinese Medicine (since 2023) · Associate Professor (2021–2023) · Visiting scholar, University of Minnesota Medical School (2019–2020) · Lecturer (2015–2018) · PhD in Basic Medicine, Wuhan University (2014)
story: Zhenpeng Qiu was senior author of a 2026 Atlas study on tacrolimus, a drug given after organ transplants to stop the immune system from rejecting the new organ (GAO2026). Over years of use, tacrolimus slowly damages the kidneys. In mice and kidney cells, the team found that astragaloside IV, a compound from the medicinal plant Astragalus, protected the kidney by turning down mTOR. With mTOR quieter, the transcription factor TFEB moved into the nucleus and switched on autophagy, the cell's recycling system, which tacrolimus had suppressed. The authors point to the mTOR-TFEB-GADD45alpha axis as a possible drug target. This is preclinical work, with no data from patients.

Qiu trained in pharmacy at South-Central Minzu University and earned a PhD in Basic Medicine at Wuhan University in 2014. Qiu joined the School of Pharmacy at Hubei University of Chinese Medicine as a lecturer in 2015, spent 2019 to 2020 as a visiting scholar at the University of Minnesota Medical School, and became a professor and doctoral supervisor in 2023.

According to the university profile, Qiu's group works on the molecular pharmacology and toxicology of natural medicines and traditional Chinese medicine, with a main focus on chronic liver disease: fatty liver disease, the inflammatory form called steatohepatitis, and liver cancer that grows out of it, as well as fatty acid metabolism in metabolic disease.

highlights.GAO2026: Senior author: led the mouse and cell study showing that astragaloside IV protects the kidney from tacrolimus by lowering mTOR and restoring TFEB-driven autophagy.

Zhang Jingyue.lab_name: School of Pharmacy, Lanzhou University (Lanzhou, China)
Zhang Jingyue.role: Pharmacy researcher at Lanzhou University working with Wen Li on the chemistry and actions of traditional Chinese medicines, from extracting plant compounds to testing a herbal formula in breast cancer models
Zhang Jingyue.sub: School of Pharmacy, Lanzhou University (papers with Wen Li, 2024–2026; at the time of the study)
story: Jingyue Zhang was first author of a 2026 Atlas study on the Xingxiao Pill, a traditional Chinese herbal formula, in breast cancer models (ZHANG2026C). The pill slowed the growth of 4T1 mouse breast cancer cells in culture and of 4T1 tumours in mice. It lowered signalling along the ErbB3/PI3K/AKT/mTOR chain, a relay that carries growth signals from the cell surface down to mTOR, the cell's growth-control kinase, and it changed how the tumours used amino acids. Computer docking pointed to two of the pill's ingredients, cinnamic acid and palmitic acid, as compounds that can bind mTOR. All of this was done in mouse cells and mice, so it does not show an effect in patients.

Zhang's other papers from the School of Pharmacy at Lanzhou University, also with Wen Li as senior author, are on the chemistry side of plant medicines. A 2024 study in Food Chemistry, for example, built magnetic molecularly imprinted polymers, a kind of chemical trap shaped to fit one molecule, to pull the compound glabridin out of licorice waste left over from industrial processing.
No personal institutional page was found, so the position shown is the Lanzhou University affiliation on the Atlas paper.

highlights.ZHANG2026C: First author: showed in 4T1 cells and mice that the Xingxiao Pill slows breast tumour growth with lower ErbB3/PI3K/AKT/mTOR signalling and changed amino acid metabolism.

Zhang Jingyue.note: Common name. PubMed also has a Jingyue Zhang at Xi'an Jiaotong University (PMID 42323314) who is a different person or cannot be tied; not used.

Heberle AM.lab_name: Institute of Biochemistry, University of Innsbruck (Innsbruck, Tyrol, Austria)
Heberle AM.role: Cell biologist and Junior Group Leader at the University of Innsbruck who studies how mTOR balances growth signalling and metabolism when cells are under stress, trained in Kathrin Thedieck's systems-biology group
Heberle AM.sub: Junior Group Leader and postdoctoral researcher, Institute of Biochemistry, University of Innsbruck · earlier in the Thedieck group, Section Systems Medicine of Metabolism and Signaling, University Medical Center Groningen (papers 2016–2021)
story: Alexander Heberle is a co-author of two Atlas studies from Kathrin Thedieck's group. The 2016 study (DAL2016) combined lab experiments with a computer model of the signalling network. It found that when amino acids are given back to starved cells, AMPK, the cell's energy-shortage sensor, switches on at the same time as mTOR, even though the two are usually described as opposites. AMPK then helps keep autophagy, the cell's recycling system, running through the kinase ULK1. The 2021 Cell paper (PRE2021) found a new brake on mTORC1, the growth-control complex: two proteins called G3BP1 and G3BP2, best known from stress granules, sit on the surface of the lysosome and hold the TSC complex there, so that TSC can keep mTORC1 in check. Without G3BPs, mTORC1 overreacts to nutrients and insulin. Both studies were mainly done in cultured cells.

Heberle's publication list follows the same line of questions: how stress switches mTOR on and off (a 2014 review), how the mitotic kinase PLK1 inhibits mTORC1 and promotes autophagy (2017), how the PI3K and p38 pathways control stress granule assembly (2019), and reviews on mTORC1 and stress granules in aging and on systems approaches to mTOR signalling (2021). Collaborations extend to cardiac IGF-1 receptor signalling and mass spectrometry methods.

PubMed lists Heberle at the University Medical Center Groningen on both Atlas papers. The current University of Innsbruck page lists Heberle as a Junior Group Leader at the Institute of Biochemistry, with a lab that studies how cells survive stress by balancing signalling and metabolism, with mTOR at the centre, and that aims to develop treatments for mTOR- and stress-related diseases.

highlights.DAL2016: Co-author of the systems study showing that amino acids switch on AMPK and mTOR at the same time in starved-then-fed cells.
highlights.PRE2021: Co-author of the Cell study showing that G3BP proteins hold the TSC complex on lysosomes and so restrain mTORC1.

Heberle AM.note: PhD institution and year not given on the Innsbruck pages.

Manifava M.lab_name: Ktistakis Group, Signalling Programme, Babraham Institute (Cambridge, England, United Kingdom)
Manifava M.role: Cell biologist in Nicholas Ktistakis's group at the Babraham Institute whose live-cell imaging work spans more than two decades of research on lipid signalling, autophagosome formation and mTORC1
Manifava M.sub: Ktistakis Group, Signalling Programme, Babraham Institute (papers 2001–2026)
story: Maria Manifava was first author of the 2016 eLife study (MAN2016) that filmed mTORC1, the growth-control complex, in living human cells as amino acids were added back after starvation. mTORC1 arrived on lysosomes, the cell's recycling compartments, within about 2 minutes and peaked by 5 minutes, in step with the amino acid leucine reaching the inside of the lysosomes. The chemical marks that mTORC1 places on its usual target proteins appeared later. The authors suggested that mTORC1 makes a short stop at the lysosome to be switched on and then acts on its targets elsewhere in the cell. Timing like this is hard to see with methods that only take snapshots, which is why live imaging mattered here. The work was done in cultured cells.

Manifava has published with Nicholas Ktistakis at the Babraham Institute in Cambridge since at least 2001, when PubMed lists a paper on the lipid-binding FYVE-domain proteins FENS-1 and DFCP1. DFCP1 became central to a 2008 study in the Journal of Cell Biology, on which Manifava is a co-author, that described the omegasome: a membrane platform rich in the lipid phosphatidylinositol 3-phosphate, connected to the endoplasmic reticulum, from which autophagosomes grow. The group's most recent paper, in Nature Communications in 2026 with Roger Williams's group at the MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology, describes a positive feedback loop between GABARAP and the PI3-kinase complex that helps autophagosome membranes expand quickly.
PubMed still lists Manifava in the Signalling Programme at the Babraham Institute on the 2026 paper. No personal page was found, so the exact job title is not shown.

highlights.MAN2016: First author: imaged living human cells to show that mTORC1 reaches lysosomes within 2 minutes of amino acid addition and acts on its targets after it leaves.

Manifava M.note: Job title not confirmed (no personal Babraham page found).

Gile B.lab_name: Research and Development Lab, Simmaron Research (Milwaukee, Wisconsin, USA)
Gile B.role: Researcher in Simmaron Research's laboratory in Milwaukee who works on low-dose rapamycin as a possible treatment for ME/CFS and led the 2026 analysis of its effects on purine metabolism
Gile B.sub: Research and Development Lab, Simmaron Research, at the University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee (papers 2025–2026)
story: ME/CFS (myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome) is a long-term illness with severe fatigue that gets worse after effort. Simmaron Research, a non-profit research group, has been testing whether low doses of rapamycin, a drug that blocks mTOR, can ease it. Brooke Gile was first author of the 2026 Atlas study from this programme (GIL2026). In patients who improved on rapamycin, blood levels of several purines, small molecules used to build DNA and carry energy, shifted in a pattern that fits lower activity of the enzyme IMP dehydrogenase in white blood cells. In lab experiments, the same purine changes harmed mitochondria and made microglia, the brain's immune cells, more inflammatory.

The study had no placebo group, so it cannot show that rapamycin caused the improvement in fatigue. The links to mitochondria and microglia come from lab tests and were not measured in the patients themselves.

Gile was also a co-author of the first paper from the same trial, published in 2025, which reported that 6 mg of rapamycin a week was tolerated without serious side effects and that most patients who stayed in the study reported less fatigue, with blood markers suggesting better autophagy, the cell's recycling system. PubMed lists Gile at the Simmaron Research and Development Lab at the University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee in that paper. No personal page was found, so training and job title are not shown.

highlights.GIL2026: First author: linked rapamycin response in an uncontrolled ME/CFS pilot to shifts in blood purines and tested the purine effects on mitochondria and microglia in the lab.

Gile B.note: PubMed author 'Gile BC' (Bridget C. Gile, Stanford water policy) is a different person; excluded.

Feng X.lab_name: State Key Laboratory of Oral Diseases, West China Hospital of Stomatology, Sichuan University (Chengdu, Sichuan, China)
Feng X.role: Researcher at the State Key Laboratory of Oral Diseases in Chengdu whose group studies how cells in the mouth respond to stress, from chemotherapy tolerance in oral cancer to inflammation in gum disease
Feng X.sub: State Key Laboratory of Oral Diseases and Research Unit of Oral Carcinogenesis and Management, West China Hospital of Stomatology, Sichuan University (papers 2025–2026; at the time of the study)
story: Xiaodong Feng was senior author of a 2026 Atlas study on why some cancer cells survive cisplatin, a widely used chemotherapy drug (RAO2026). The team ran a genome-wide CRISPR screen, switching off genes one by one across the genome to see which ones change how cells cope with the drug. The surprise was that blocking mTOR, the growth-control kinase, made the cells more tolerant of cisplatin, not less, because it switched on protective autophagy, the cell's recycling system. The amino acid transporter SLC7A5, which brings leucine and other large amino acids into the cell, sat at the centre of this circuit. Adding extra leucine made tumour cells carrying SLC7A5 sensitive to cisplatin again. The work was done in cancer cells and tumour models, not in patients.
The finding matters for drug combinations: mTOR inhibitors are sometimes proposed alongside chemotherapy, and this study suggests that in some tumours they could do the opposite of what is hoped.

PubMed lists Feng at the State Key Laboratory of Oral Diseases, West China Hospital of Stomatology, Sichuan University. A 2025 paper from the same laboratory in International Immunopharmacology, with Pengcheng Rao among the co-authors, showed that a stress response in the gum-lining cells drives inflammation and bone loss in periodontitis. No personal institutional page could be checked, so further details of training and title are not shown.

highlights.RAO2026: Senior author: led the CRISPR screen study showing that mTOR inhibition can protect cancer cells from cisplatin through autophagy, with SLC7A5 and leucine as a way to reverse it.

Rao P.lab_name: State Key Laboratory of Oral Diseases, West China Hospital of Stomatology, Sichuan University (Chengdu, Sichuan, China)
Rao P.role: Researcher at the West China Hospital of Stomatology in Chengdu who led a genome-wide CRISPR screen showing that switching off mTOR can help cancer cells tolerate cisplatin
Rao P.sub: State Key Laboratory of Oral Diseases, West China Hospital of Stomatology, Sichuan University (papers with Xiaodong Feng, 2025–2026; at the time of the study)
story: Pengcheng Rao was first author of the 2026 Atlas study on cisplatin tolerance (RAO2026). Cisplatin is a platinum chemotherapy drug used against many cancers, including cancers of the head and neck. Using a genome-wide CRISPR screen, which knocks out genes one at a time across the whole genome, the team asked which genes change how well cancer cells survive the drug. Blocking mTOR, the growth-control kinase, helped the cells survive, because it turned on autophagy, a recycling process that protected them. The amino acid transporter SLC7A5 linked nutrient supply to this response, and giving extra leucine, one of the amino acids it carries, made SLC7A5-expressing tumour cells sensitive to cisplatin again. This was shown in cancer cells and tumour models, not in patients.

Rao also appears, with Xiaodong Feng as a co-author, on a 2025 paper from the same State Key Laboratory of Oral Diseases on how stressed gum-lining cells drive inflammation in periodontitis. No personal page was found, so the position shown is the affiliation on the Atlas paper.

highlights.RAO2026: First author: ran the genome-wide CRISPR screen showing that mTOR inhibition promotes cisplatin tolerance through autophagy and that leucine can reverse it in SLC7A5-expressing cells.

Yang HJ.lab_name: Structural Biology Program, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (New York, New York, USA)
Yang HJ.role: Researcher in Nikola Pavletich's structural biology laboratory at Memorial Sloan Kettering and co-author of the two Nature papers that showed the atomic structure of mTOR and of mTORC1
Yang HJ.sub: Structural Biology Program, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (Pavletich laboratory, papers 2013 and 2017; at the time of the studies)
story: Hyo J Yang is a co-author of two structure papers from Nikola Pavletich's laboratory at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center that changed how mTOR is pictured. Structural biology works out the exact 3D shape of a protein, atom by atom, which shows how it does its job and how drugs fit into it.

The 2013 paper (YAN2013) solved the crystal structure of the mTOR kinase, the part of the protein that adds phosphate groups to its targets. It showed that the active site sits in a deep, narrow cleft, guarded by a section called the FRB domain that acts like a gatekeeper for incoming target proteins. That explained why rapamycin, which binds the FRB domain together with its partner protein FKBP12, blocks mTOR by limiting access to the cleft, and why cancer-causing mutations cluster where they do. The 2017 paper (YAN2017) used cryo-electron microscopy, which images frozen protein complexes with an electron beam, to show the whole mTORC1 complex. It showed how the small protein RHEB, which signals growth, bends mTORC1 into its active shape, and how the inhibitor PRAS40 blocks it. Both papers describe purified proteins, not cells or animals.

These two papers are the only PubMed records for Yang with Pavletich, and no other publication or institutional page could be firmly tied to this name, which is common. The affiliation shown is the one on the papers. Hyo J Yang is a different person from Haijuan Yang, first author of both papers.

highlights.YAN2013: Co-author of the crystal structure of the mTOR kinase, which showed the deep active-site cleft guarded by the FRB domain.
highlights.YAN2017: Co-author of the cryo-EM structures showing how RHEB switches mTORC1 on and how PRAS40 blocks it.

Medina DL.lab_name: Telethon Institute of Genetics and Medicine (TIGEM) and Department of Translational Medical Science, University of Naples Federico II (Pozzuoli, Campania, Italy)
Medina DL.role: Cell biologist at the Telethon Institute of Genetics and Medicine in Naples who showed how TFEB, the master switch for lysosome genes, is controlled by calcium released from lysosomes, and who works on lysosomal storage diseases
Medina DL.sub: Telethon Institute of Genetics and Medicine (TIGEM), Pozzuoli · Department of Translational Medical Science, University of Naples Federico II (papers 2011–2026)
story: Diego Medina is a co-author of the 2012 EMBO Journal paper from Andrea Ballabio's group at TIGEM (SET2012) that showed how the lysosome, the cell's recycling compartment, talks to the nucleus. When nutrients are plentiful, mTORC1, the growth-control complex, sits on the lysosome surface and adds a phosphate group to the transcription factor TFEB, which keeps TFEB outside the nucleus. When mTORC1 is blocked, when the cell is starved, or when lysosomes are under stress, TFEB moves into the nucleus and switches on genes for new lysosomes and for autophagy. The study was done in cultured cells and gave a simple explanation of how cells match their recycling capacity to their needs.

Medina's own first-author papers fill in other parts of the TFEB story. A 2011 Developmental Cell paper showed that TFEB also drives lysosomal exocytosis, in which lysosomes fuse with the cell surface and empty their contents outside, and that this cleared stored material in models of lysosomal storage diseases. A 2015 Nature Cell Biology paper showed that calcium released from the lysosome through the channel MCOLN1 switches on the phosphatase calcineurin, which removes the phosphate that mTORC1 put on TFEB, so TFEB can enter the nucleus. In mice this route was needed for TFEB activation during starvation and exercise.

PubMed lists Medina at TIGEM in Pozzuoli, near Naples, on more than 50 papers, and in 2026 also at the Department of Translational Medical Science of the University of Naples Federico II, on work on autophagy and inflammation in intestinal organoids from people with coeliac disease.

highlights.SET2012: Co-author of the study showing that mTORC1 phosphorylates TFEB on the lysosome and that blocking mTORC1 sends TFEB into the nucleus to switch on lysosome genes.

Hands JM.lab_name: Department of Pathology, University of Southern California (Los Angeles, California, USA)
Hands JM.role: Researcher in integrative medicine and nutrition science, trained at George Washington University, who wrote a cautious review of whether off-label rapamycin is justified for healthy adults
Hands JM.sub: Department of Pathology, University of Southern California (2026 paper) · earlier at the George Washington University School of Medicine and Health Sciences (2025)
story: Jacob Hands was first author of a 2025 review in Aging (HAN2025) that asked a direct question: what does the human evidence say about taking low-dose rapamycin, or related mTOR-blocking drugs, to slow aging in healthy adults? Some people already take rapamycin off-label for this reason, based mostly on animal studies in which it lengthened life. The review collected the clinical studies and re-analysed one group of people using PhenoAge, a 'biological age' score calculated from routine blood tests.

Its verdict was careful. The animal data on lifespan are strong, but the human studies are small, short and use different doses and measures, and they have not shown that rapamycin slows aging in healthy people. The review is useful as a reminder of the gap between results in mice and evidence in people.

PubMed lists Hands at the George Washington University School of Medicine and Health Sciences on the 2025 review. A 2026 narrative review in Nutrients, on common genetic variants that affect blood fats and heart disease risk and how diet might interact with them, lists Hands at the Department of Pathology of the University of Southern California, with co-authors from George Washington University's Office of Integrative Medicine and Health. No personal page was found to confirm job title or training.

highlights.HAN2025: First author: reviewed the human evidence for off-label rapamycin in healthy adults and concluded that it does not yet show a slowing of aging.

Hands JM.note: Move from GWU to USC is based on the 2026 Nutrients affiliation only (same full name, GWU co-authors); role at USC unknown.

Astle CM.lab_name: Harrison Laboratory, The Jackson Laboratory (Bar Harbor, Maine, USA)
Astle CM.role: Long-time research associate of David Harrison at The Jackson Laboratory, with work on mouse blood stem cells and aging since the 1970s, and a co-author of the Interventions Testing Program papers that showed rapamycin extends mouse lifespan
Astle CM.sub: The Jackson Laboratory, Bar Harbor, Maine (papers with David E. Harrison, 1976–2019)
story: C. Michael Astle is a co-author of five Atlas papers from the Interventions Testing Program (ITP) of the US National Institute on Aging. The ITP tests drugs and supplements for effects on lifespan in genetically mixed mice, running the same experiment at three sites (The Jackson Laboratory, the University of Michigan and UT Health San Antonio) so that a result has to hold up in all three. The 2009 Nature paper (HAR2009) showed that rapamycin, a drug that blocks mTOR, extended lifespan even when started late in life at about 600 days of age. Later papers showed that the gain depends on dose and is larger in females (MIL2011, MIL2014), that acarbose and 17-alpha-estradiol extend life mainly in males (HAR2014), and that resveratrol, green tea extract, curcumin and several other popular compounds did not change lifespan (STR2012). Publishing negative results was part of the programme's design. All of this is mouse work.

Astle has worked with David Harrison at The Jackson Laboratory in Bar Harbor, Maine, for decades. Their first joint PubMed paper, on immune-cell responses in mice, dates from 1976, and PubMed lists more than 50 papers by the two together. Their most recent joint paper in PubMed, from 2019, reported that adding glycine to the diet modestly extended lifespan in ITP mice. On that paper the name appears in full as C Michael Astle, at The Jackson Laboratory.

highlights.STR2012: Co-author of the ITP paper that found no lifespan effect from resveratrol, green tea extract, curcumin, oxaloacetic acid or medium-chain triglyceride oil.
highlights.HAR2014: Co-author of the ITP paper in which acarbose, 17-alpha-estradiol and NDGA extended lifespan, mainly in males.
highlights.MIL2011: Co-author of the ITP paper in which rapamycin extended lifespan but resveratrol and simvastatin did not.
highlights.MIL2014: Co-author of the ITP paper showing that rapamycin's lifespan effect depends on dose and sex.
highlights.HAR2009: Co-author of the Nature paper showing that rapamycin fed late in life extends lifespan in genetically mixed mice.

Flurkey K.lab_name: The Jackson Laboratory (Bar Harbor, Maine, USA)
Flurkey K.role: Biologist of aging at The Jackson Laboratory who has studied mouse lifespan and hormones since the early 1980s and co-authored the Interventions Testing Program papers on rapamycin
Flurkey K.sub: The Jackson Laboratory, Bar Harbor, Maine (papers 2009–2025) · earlier work on reproductive aging in mice with Caleb Finch (1982)
story: Kevin Flurkey is a co-author of four Atlas papers from the National Institute on Aging Interventions Testing Program (ITP), which tests possible anti-aging drugs in genetically mixed mice at three sites at once. The 2009 Nature paper (HAR2009) showed that rapamycin, a drug that blocks mTOR, extended mouse lifespan even when it was started late in life. Follow-up papers showed that resveratrol and simvastatin did not extend life in the same experiment (MIL2011), that rapamycin's effect grows with dose and is larger in females (MIL2014), and that acarbose, 17-alpha-estradiol and NDGA extend lifespan mainly in males (HAR2014). These are mouse results; whether they carry over to people is still open.

Flurkey's PubMed record goes back to 1982, with a paper with Caleb Finch on how levels of the reproductive hormones LH, progesterone and prolactin change with age in female C57BL/6J mice. At The Jackson Laboratory, Flurkey has worked on mouse aging with David Harrison's group, including the ITP studies and, more recently, genetic studies of lifespan in Diversity Outbred mice, a genetically mixed mouse population. A 2025 paper in Genetics, with Gary Churchill's group and Calico Life Sciences, combined three such studies with 2,444 mice and found eight regions of the genome that affect lifespan.

Sills AM.lab_name: Barshop Institute for Longevity and Aging Studies, UT Health San Antonio (San Antonio, Texas, USA)
Sills AM.role: Researcher at the Barshop Institute in San Antonio who worked with common marmosets in Adam Salmon's group and led the 2018 study of long-term rapamycin and blood health in these small primates
Sills AM.sub: Barshop Institute for Longevity and Aging Studies, UT Health San Antonio (papers 2018–2020; at the time of the study)
story: Aubrey Sills was first author of the 2018 Atlas study (SIL2018), with Adam Salmon as senior author, that gave middle-aged common marmosets rapamycin every day for nine months. Marmosets are small, relatively short-lived monkeys, which makes them useful for testing anti-aging drugs in a primate. Rapamycin blocks mTOR and extends life in mice, and the study asked whether long-term use is safe for the blood system of a primate. In the marmosets, routine blood tests changed only a little. Females had lower rapamycin levels in their blood than males, yet both sexes showed few changes. The authors concluded that blood side effects are unlikely with long-term rapamycin in healthy middle-aged animals of this kind. This is a primate study, not a human one.

Sills also co-authored a 2020 paper in GeroScience from the same institute, with Veronica Galvan and Adam Salmon, that described a method for growing nerve cells and astrocytes from newborn marmoset brains, as a primate model for studying brain aging in a dish. No personal page was found, so the affiliation shown is the one on these papers.

highlights.SIL2018: First author: reported that nine months of daily rapamycin caused only minor changes in blood counts in middle-aged marmosets.

Curatolo P.lab_name: Child Neurology and Psychiatry Unit, Systems Medicine Department, Tor Vergata University (Rome, Italy)
Curatolo P.role: Child neurologist at Tor Vergata University in Rome who has spent much of a long career on tuberous sclerosis complex, the genetic disease of overactive mTOR, with a focus on epilepsy and brain development in children
Curatolo P.sub: Child Neurology and Psychiatry Unit, Systems Medicine Department, Tor Vergata University, Rome · Tor Vergata University Hospital (EXIST-3, 2016)
story: Tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC) is a genetic disease caused by faulty TSC1 or TSC2 genes. These genes normally act as a brake on mTORC1, the growth-control complex, so in TSC mTORC1 runs too high and benign growths form in the brain, kidneys, skin and other organs. Many children with TSC have epilepsy that standard drugs do not control. Paolo Curatolo is a co-author of EXIST-3 (FRE2016), a phase 3, double-blind trial published in the Lancet in 2016 that tested whether everolimus, a drug that blocks mTOR, could reduce these seizures.

The trial enrolled 366 patients aged 2 to 65 with treatment-resistant focal seizures and randomly assigned them to placebo, a low everolimus dose or a high everolimus dose. About 15% of patients on placebo had their seizures cut by half or more, against 28% on the low dose and 40% on the high dose. Because the drug targets the cause of the disease and not just the seizures, EXIST-3 is one of the clearest examples in people of what blocking mTOR can do.

PubMed lists Curatolo on more than 140 papers about tuberous sclerosis. A 2025 review in eBioMedicine, written with colleagues in Rome and Amsterdam, sets out how biomarkers such as EEG findings, gene variants and brain imaging can pick out infants at high risk, and how early treatment with vigabatrin or mTOR inhibitors might prevent the severe epilepsy and developmental problems that often follow. On that paper Curatolo is listed at the Child Neurology and Psychiatry Unit, Systems Medicine Department, Tor Vergata University.

highlights.FRE2016: Co-author of the phase 3 EXIST-3 trial showing that everolimus reduces treatment-resistant seizures in tuberous sclerosis complex.

de Cabo R.lab_name: Translational Gerontology Branch, National Institute on Aging Intramural Research Program, National Institutes of Health (Baltimore, Maryland, USA)
de Cabo R.role: Aging researcher at the US National Institute on Aging who has studied calorie restriction, fasting and drugs that mimic them in mice and rhesus monkeys, including the long-running NIA monkey study
de Cabo R.sub: Translational Gerontology Branch, National Institute on Aging Intramural Research Program, NIH, Baltimore (papers to 2026)
story: Rafael de Cabo is a co-author of the 2017 Nature Communications paper (MAT2017) that put side by side the two longest studies of calorie restriction in primates: one run by the National Institute on Aging (NIA) and one at the University of Wisconsin. Calorie restriction, eating 10 to 40% less while still getting all nutrients, lengthens life in many animals, and part of its effect is thought to run through lower mTOR activity. The two monkey studies had seemed to disagree on survival. Comparing them directly, the authors found clear health benefits in both, while the effect on survival depended on study design and on what the control monkeys were fed. This is evidence from rhesus monkeys, the closest animal model to humans for this question.

De Cabo was also the senior author of the 2012 Nature paper, with Julie Mattison as first author, that first reported that calorie restriction in the NIA monkeys had not improved survival, in contrast to the Wisconsin study. That apparent clash is what the 2017 comparison resolved. PubMed lists more than 400 papers under the name, many on how diet, fasting and candidate drugs affect health and lifespan in mice.

De Cabo works in the Translational Gerontology Branch of the NIA Intramural Research Program in Baltimore, and recent 2026 papers with collaborators in Madrid and at the NIA cover aging of the blood system and of human skeletal muscle.

highlights.MAT2017: Co-author of the comparison of the NIA and Wisconsin rhesus monkey studies, which showed consistent health benefits of calorie restriction and survival effects that depended on study design.

Mattison JA.lab_name: Translational Gerontology Branch, National Institute on Aging Intramural Research Program, National Institutes of Health (Baltimore, Maryland, USA)
Mattison JA.role: Primate aging researcher at the US National Institute on Aging who led the NIA study of calorie restriction in rhesus monkeys and its comparison with the Wisconsin study
Mattison JA.sub: Translational Gerontology Branch, National Institute on Aging Intramural Research Program, NIH (papers to 2026) · Laboratory of Experimental Gerontology, NIA, NIH Animal Center, Dickerson, Maryland (2012)
story: Julie Mattison was first author of the 2017 Nature Communications paper (MAT2017) that compared the two long-term studies of calorie restriction in rhesus monkeys, one at the National Institute on Aging (NIA) and one at the University of Wisconsin. Eating less without malnutrition extends life in many animals, and lower mTOR activity is one of the routes thought to explain it. The two monkey studies had reached different conclusions about survival. Looking at both data sets together, the authors found consistent health benefits, while the survival effect depended on study design and on the diet of the control animals. This is evidence from monkeys, not from people.

Mattison was also first author of the 2012 Nature paper reporting that calorie restriction had not improved survival in the NIA monkeys, at that time listed at the Laboratory of Experimental Gerontology at the NIH Animal Center in Dickerson, Maryland, with Rafael de Cabo as senior author. That result, at odds with the Wisconsin study, set up the 2017 comparison.

In the Atlas, Mattison is also a co-author of a 2021 study (HOR2021) that built epigenetic clocks for the common marmoset, a small monkey, and found that rapamycin did not significantly change epigenetic age in these animals. PubMed lists Mattison at the NIA Translational Gerontology Branch on more recent papers, including a 2026 preprint on muscle aging that used cells from old and young rhesus monkeys.

highlights.MAT2017: First author: led the direct comparison of the NIA and Wisconsin rhesus monkey calorie restriction studies.
highlights.HOR2021: Co-author of the marmoset study that built epigenetic clocks and found no significant effect of rapamycin on epigenetic age.

Guerrero-Morín JG.lab_name: Unidad Monterrey, Centro de Investigación y de Estudios Avanzados del IPN (Apodaca, Nuevo León, Mexico)
Guerrero-Morín JG.role: Researcher at the Monterrey unit of Cinvestav in Mexico and first author of a 2020 mathematical model of how mTORC1 could tune the body's daily clock
Guerrero-Morín JG.sub: Unidad Monterrey, Centro de Investigación y de Estudios Avanzados del IPN (Cinvestav), Apodaca, Nuevo León (at the time of the study, 2020)
story: Almost every cell in the body runs a circadian clock, a loop of genes and proteins that rises and falls over about 24 hours. One of the central clock proteins is BMAL1. mTORC1, the growth-control complex, is one of the signals thought to affect the clock through BMAL1. José Guerrero-Morín was first author of a 2020 paper in the Journal of Theoretical Biology (GUE2020) that turned these observations into a mathematical model.

The model suggests that mTORC1 makes the clock's swings bigger by boosting the making (translation) of BMAL1, and changes the length of each cycle by controlling where BMAL1 sits inside the cell. Both effects together were needed for a strong, regular rhythm in the model. This is a computer model, not an experiment: it makes predictions that still have to be tested in cells or animals. It matters for the Atlas because it gives a testable picture of how growth signalling and daily timing might be linked.

The paper was written at the Monterrey unit of Cinvestav, a national research centre in Mexico, with Santillán as senior author. PubMed lists no other papers under this name, so later career steps could not be traced.

highlights.GUE2020: First author: built a mathematical model in which mTORC1 sets circadian clock amplitude through BMAL1 translation and period through BMAL1 location.

Guerrero-Morín JG.note: Only one PubMed record; later career not traced.

Wilkinson JE.lab_name: Unit for Laboratory Animal Medicine and Department of Pathology, University of Michigan (Ann Arbor, Michigan, USA)
Wilkinson JE.role: Pathologist at the University of Michigan who examines animal tissues for aging and cancer studies, and first author of the 2012 paper showing that rapamycin slows many signs of aging in mice
Wilkinson JE.sub: Unit for Laboratory Animal Medicine and Department of Pathology, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor (papers 2012–2026)
story: When rapamycin was shown to lengthen mouse lifespan in 2009, a key question remained: did it slow aging itself, or did it simply delay the cancers that kill most laboratory mice? John Wilkinson was first author of the 2012 Aging Cell paper (WIL2012), with Richard Miller as senior author, that tackled this question by looking closely at many tissues. A pathologist studies tissue under the microscope to find disease and damage.

In mice given rapamycin, age-related changes in the heart, liver, adrenal glands, endometrium and tendon developed more slowly, and the age-related fall in spontaneous activity was smaller. The paper also reported harms: treated mice had more testicular degeneration and more cataracts. Because the benefits showed up across many organs, beyond a drop in tumours, the authors argued that rapamycin slows aging more broadly. These results are from mice.

PubMed lists Wilkinson at the University of Michigan in Ann Arbor on dozens of papers, often as the pathologist on mouse studies from other groups. The most recent, from 2026 in Nature Immunology, is a study from Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory on how the fat-sensing factor PPAR-delta changes the balance between cancer cells and immune cells.

highlights.WIL2012: First author: showed that rapamycin slows age-related change in heart, liver, adrenal gland, endometrium and tendon in mice, while increasing cataracts and testicular degeneration.

Munaretto GM.lab_name: Department of Medicine, Universidade do Contestado (Concordia, Brazil)
Munaretto GM.role: Member of the Department of Medicine at Universidade do Contestado in Santa Catarina, Brazil, and senior author of a 2026 meta-analysis of everolimus after heart transplantation
Munaretto GM.sub: Department of Medicine, Universidade do Contestado, Concórdia, Santa Catarina (papers 2026; at the time of the study)
story: After a heart transplant, patients take drugs for life to stop the immune system from attacking the new heart. The standard drugs, calcineurin inhibitors such as tacrolimus, can damage the kidneys, and over the years many transplanted hearts develop cardiac allograft vasculopathy, a thickening of the coronary arteries. Everolimus blocks mTOR, which slows the growth of immune cells and of the cells in artery walls. Giancarlo Maruri Munaretto was senior author of a 2026 meta-analysis in JHLT Open (VITTE2026) that pooled 60 studies with 1,786 heart transplant recipients to weigh up everolimus.

A meta-analysis combines the results of many separate studies to get a clearer overall answer. Here, everolimus-based treatment slowed the artery thickening seen on intravascular ultrasound and kept kidney function better when the dose of calcineurin inhibitors was lowered. Deaths were about the same, but side effects and stopping the drug were more common. The study draws on data from people, so it speaks directly to patient care.

PubMed lists Munaretto at the Department of Medicine of Universidade do Contestado in Concordia, Santa Catarina, Brazil, as senior author of one other 2026 meta-analysis, on sealing the needle track with saline to prevent a collapsed lung after CT-guided lung biopsy. No personal page was found to show career stage.

highlights.VITTE2026: Senior author of the meta-analysis showing that everolimus slows cardiac allograft vasculopathy and protects kidney function after heart transplantation, with more side effects.

Munaretto GM.note: Career stage unknown; no personal page found. lab_name uses canonical 'Concordia, Brazil' without accent.

Yao JC.lab_name: Department of Gastrointestinal Medical Oncology, The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center (Houston, Texas, USA)
Yao JC.role: Medical oncologist at MD Anderson Cancer Center who led the RADIANT-3 and RADIANT-4 trials that made the mTOR inhibitor everolimus a standard treatment for advanced neuroendocrine tumours
Yao JC.sub: Department of Gastrointestinal Medical Oncology, The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center, Houston (papers 2011–2026)
story: Neuroendocrine tumours grow from hormone-making cells, for example in the pancreas, gut or lung. They often grow slowly, but once they spread they are hard to treat, and in many of them the PI3K-AKT-mTOR pathway is switched on. James Yao was first author of RADIANT-3 (YAO2011), a phase 3 trial in the New England Journal of Medicine that randomly assigned 410 patients with advanced pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours to everolimus, an mTOR-blocking drug, or placebo. The time before the cancer grew again more than doubled, from a median of 4.6 months on placebo to 11.0 months on everolimus, and most side effects were mild. The result led to everolimus being approved for this cancer.

Yao then led RADIANT-4, published in the Lancet in 2016, which tested everolimus in 302 patients with non-functional neuroendocrine tumours of the lung or gastrointestinal tract. Median progression-free survival was 11.0 months with everolimus and 3.9 months with placebo. Together the two trials showed that blocking mTOR helps across neuroendocrine tumours from several organs, which is strong evidence from people that mTOR signalling drives these cancers.

PubMed lists Yao at The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center throughout this work and, in 2026, in its Department of Gastrointestinal Medical Oncology, with more than 120 papers on neuroendocrine tumours.

highlights.YAO2011: First author of the RADIANT-3 trial showing that everolimus more than doubles progression-free survival in advanced pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours.

Orozco JM.lab_name: Sabatini Laboratory, Whitehead Institute for Biomedical Research (Cambridge, Massachusetts, USA)
Orozco JM.role: Researcher trained in David Sabatini's laboratory at the Whitehead Institute and MIT who showed that mTORC1 senses glucose through the glycolysis metabolite DHAP
Orozco JM.sub: Whitehead Institute for Biomedical Research and Department of Biology, Massachusetts Institute of Technology (Sabatini laboratory, papers 2014–2021; at the time of the studies)
story: Jose Orozco is a co-author of four Atlas papers from David Sabatini's laboratory at the Whitehead Institute that mapped how mTORC1, the growth-control complex, learns what nutrients a cell has. Sestrin proteins bind the GATOR2 complex to dampen amino acid signalling (CHA2014). A complex named KICSTOR holds the GATOR1 brake at the lysosome so that nutrients can control mTORC1 (WOL2017). A protein named SAMTOR senses S-adenosylmethionine, a molecule made from the amino acid methionine (GU2017), which links mTORC1 to diet in a way that may matter for why methionine restriction affects aging. And genome-wide CRISPR screens showed that the kinases AMPK and HRI relay mitochondrial problems to mTORC1 (CON2021). These are laboratory studies, mostly in cultured cells.

Orozco's own first-author paper, in Nature Metabolism in 2020, answered a question the field had left open: how mTORC1 knows that glucose is present, separately from the energy sensor AMPK. Working in human cells engineered to lack AMPK, the team traced the signal to dihydroxyacetone phosphate (DHAP), a molecule made partway through glycolysis. DHAP is also a starting material for making fats, a process that mTORC1 controls, which gives a reason for the cell to watch it.

On these papers PubMed lists Orozco at the Whitehead Institute and the MIT Department of Biology, with the Koch Institute and the Broad Institute. No later position could be confirmed, so the affiliation shown is the one on the Atlas papers.

highlights.CHA2014: Co-author of the study showing that Sestrins bind GATOR2 to restrain amino acid signalling to mTORC1.
highlights.WOL2017: Co-author of the study showing that KICSTOR recruits GATOR1 to the lysosome.
highlights.GU2017: Co-author of the study identifying SAMTOR as an S-adenosylmethionine sensor for mTORC1.
highlights.CON2021: Co-author of the CRISPR screen study showing that AMPK and HRI relay mitochondrial dysfunction to mTORC1.

Orozco JM.note: Current position not found (PubMed shows no Orozco JM papers after 2021 in this field); likely MIT PhD student in Sabatini lab, but not confirmed.

Birsoy K.lab_name: Laboratory of Metabolic Regulation and Genetics, The Rockefeller University (New York, New York, USA)
Birsoy K.role: Head of the Laboratory of Metabolic Regulation and Genetics at The Rockefeller University, who earlier worked in David Sabatini's laboratory and uses genetic screens to find how cancer cells and normal cells meet their metabolic needs
Birsoy K.sub: Head of laboratory, Laboratory of Metabolic Regulation and Genetics, The Rockefeller University · earlier at the Whitehead Institute for Biomedical Research and MIT (Sabatini laboratory, papers 2012–2015)
story: Kivanç Birsoy is a co-author of two Atlas papers from David Sabatini's laboratory at the Whitehead Institute. The 2012 Nature paper (YIL2012) showed in mice that calorie restriction lowers mTORC1 activity in Paneth cells, the cells that sit next to intestinal stem cells and support them. With less mTORC1, Paneth cells send signals that make the neighbouring stem cells more numerous and more active. The 2014 Cancer Discovery paper (GRA2014) went through MTOR mutations found in human cancers, identified 33 that switch the pathway on, and showed that cancer cells carrying them were more sensitive to rapamycin in cell culture and in mouse tumour grafts. That suggests the mutations could help pick patients who might respond to mTOR inhibitors.

Birsoy's own first-author work in the Sabatini laboratory was on cell metabolism. A 2015 Cell paper used a CRISPR screen to find genes that cells need when their mitochondria are blocked by the drug phenformin. It showed that one essential job of the mitochondrial electron transport chain in dividing cells is to let them make the amino acid aspartate, and that cells without a working chain can grow if they get extra aspartate.

Birsoy now leads the Laboratory of Metabolic Regulation and Genetics at The Rockefeller University in New York. The lab continues to combine genetic screens with metabolism; a 2026 paper in Cell Chemical Biology, for example, used CRISPR screens to identify TXNDC15 as a missing part of the system that removes faulty proteins from the endoplasmic reticulum, with effects on lipid balance.

highlights.GRA2014: Co-author of the study showing that many cancer-associated MTOR mutations switch the pathway on and predict rapamycin sensitivity.
highlights.YIL2012: Co-author of the mouse study showing that calorie restriction lowers mTORC1 in Paneth cells and so boosts the neighbouring intestinal stem cells.

Birsoy K.note: PubMed spells the first name with a Turkish dotless i (Kıvanç); kept the current spelling. PhD not confirmed (web search budget ran out).
